title: John Hinckley Jr. Shares New Message to Jodie Foster, 45 Years After Trying to Assassinate Ronald Reagan to Impress Her: ‘I Wish Her Well’
description: John Hinckley Jr., the Oklahoma native who tried to assassinate President Ronald Regan in 1981 in an attempt to impress Jodie Foster, shared a new m
body:
John Hinckley Jr., the Oklahoma native who tried to assassinate President Ronald Regan in 1981 in an attempt to impress Jodie Foster, shared a new message for “The Silence of the Lambs” star during a recent appearance on the “Mark Joseph Show” (via EW).

	“I just wish Jodie Foster well, you know,” Hinckley said. “I don’t really see her movies, but I wish her well, and I know she’s doing quite well. And that’s all I can say is just, I wish Jodie well, and I hope she has a good life.”
	

	On March 30, 1981, Hinckley waited outside the Hilton Hotel in Washington, D.C., for President Regan. When President Regan emerged from the building, among a crowd of onlookers, he fired all six shots of his Röhm revolver at the commander in chief. Several of the accompanying staff and Secret Service agents were injured, and one of the bullets ricocheted off of President Reagan’s limousine and struck him in the chest. Labor official Alfred Antenucci brought Hinckley to the ground seconds after the shooting, with assistance from agent Dennis McCarthy.

	Hinckley was tried in federal court, but was found not guilty on all 13 charges by reason of insanity.

	Hinckley had stalked Foster while she was at Yale years before the assassination attempt, which was to be his final act to win her over. He was 25 at the time, while Foster was 18, and already had dozens of credits to her name, including “Taxi Driver” and “Freaky Friday.”

	When asked by host Mark Joseph what he hoped to achieve by assassinating Regan, Hinckley said, “I wanted to have a union with Jodie Foster and live the rest of my life with her and all these things that, of course, were delusional. But I was believing those things at the time, so the best outcome would have been a union with Jodie Foster.”
	

	“I thought she would, you know, after things settled down, join me wherever I was,” Hinckley added. “I wasn’t sure if I was gonna be in jail or the hospital or what after things settled down. I had this notion that she was gonna join me wherever I was.”

schema.headline: John Hinckley Jr. Shares New Message to Jodie Foster, 45 Years After Trying to Assassinate Ronald Reagan to Impress Her: ‘I Wish Her Well’

title: ‘The Brink of War’ Review: Reagan and Gorbachev Engage in Unengaging Verbal Battle
description: There was a time when talky slabs of recent political history like “The Brink of War,” carried by skilled name actors who aren’t quite stars, were l
body:
There was a time when talky slabs of recent political history like “The Brink of War,” carried by skilled name actors who aren’t quite stars, were largely the preserve of Emmy-chasing TV networks. Today, with a bit of added Christian-right rhetoric, they’re ready for the big screen, as the growing faith-based film industry expands its palette in terms of subject matter — but not cinematic style, as evidenced by this dutifully drab gray-flannel enterprise from writer-director Michael Russell Gunn.
	

	The latest from so-called “values-based” distributor Angel Studios comes hot on the heels of their Fourth of July release “Young Washington,” which has drummed up nearly $47 million in theaters, and shares with that Great Man biopic the kind of textbook American patriotism that recalls, well, a certain kind of textbook. The story of how the 1986 Reykjavik Summit between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev paved the way for the next year’s nuclear arms control treaty between the United States and the Soviet Union, it feels veritably designed (right down to its PG rating) to bore kids in history classrooms for generations to come. Adult audiences may be more willing when “The Brink of War” opens wide on Friday, but it’s doubtful they’ll be much more entertained. 


	“Young Washington” was stolidly old-fashioned, but still rousing in its gung-ho way. “The Brink of War” is a far dustier, more static affair: Its drama is all in two aging men seated at a table, arguing with each other over two days about nuclear disarmament in a remote Icelandic consulate building. That doesn’t have to be dull, of course, and if you squint a little at the screen, you can just about see the first-rate Broadway play that could emerge from this material — with no casting changes required — if the telling were just a little more tense, and the writing just a little more witty. 
	

	Gunn’s stiff script is attentive to the political dynamics and rhetorical thrust of the talks, and if its repeated emphasis on American honor, freedom and statesmanship makes for a somewhat pious exercise, you can’t deny the narrative stakes are high. The lines of conflict are established early and clearly: Where Gorbachev merely wants to discuss the banning of ballistic missiles, Reagan’s equal emphasis on human rights — in particular, the Soviet Union’s restrictions on Western travel for its citizens — complicates the discussion, while his insistence on pushing the controversial Strategic Defense Initiative continues to be a sticking point for the other side. (No surprise that the film glides over American political opposition to the latter proposal, unambiguously taking Reagan’s side on all fronts.)

	What’s crucially lacking here is a particularly compelling sense of Reagan and Gorbachev as human characters. Jeff Daniels and Jared Harris, respectively, put forward solidly recognizable impressions of the men we knew from televised speeches and newscasts, but aren’t given many notes to play: The leaders’ inner lives are limited to standard-issue exchanges with their wives about professional duty and strain, which don’t vary much in tone from the pithy aphorisms they share with their right-hand men about diplomacy, or lack thereof. Even when religion comes up for discussion, it’s in predictably on-message Angel Studios fashion, as Reagan chides his atheist opponent for “denying [his people] the hereafter.” (“This is worse than propoganda!” protests one of Gorbachev’s aides; irony is not one of the film’s stronger suits.) At one point, Reagan spills some chicken salad sandwich filling on his shirt; it’s about the most unguarded moment we get. 

	Reagan also, naturally, gets the leading perspective, as well as the most generous sounding boards in the supporting ensemble: not just his wife Nancy (Hope Davis), who doesn’t travel to Reykjavik but provides repeated counsel over the phone, but his Secretary of State George Shultz (played with an air of gruff, salt-of-the-earth decency by J.K. Simmons), on hand to straighten out Team America’s priorities when the negotiations go awry. 

	Though the film’s lens is consistently ennobling — abetted by everything from DP Magdalena Górka’s sober official-portrait lighting to Austin Wintory’s overbearing score — Daniels gets Reagan’s combination of folksy squareness and flintier social conservatism. It’s a more substantial portrayal than Dennis Quaid’s in the tackily propagandistic 2024 biopic “Reagan,” though we’re still left with the impression that, in the ranks of American presidents on screen, the erstwhile movie star remains a less dynamic movie subject.
	

	Harris, meanwhile, plays Gorbachev as an altogether more aloof, intractable and unknowable figure, which is precisely how the film wants it — though Branka Katić gives the canniest, funniest performance here as his watchful, image-conscious wife Raisa, here placed in a remote PR war with the U.S. First Lady where, yet again, America gets to come out on top. The film could use a few more such colorful secondary strands adjoining the main conflict, though one subplot involving a maybe-romance between two jaded journalists assigned to the summit is oddly framed and abruptly dropped. 

	Fairly deliberate for much of its two-hour running time, “The Brink of War” suddenly races toward a denouement in its final quarter-hour — somewhat eliding the fact that the Reykjavik Summit was, at least in the short term, a failure, with the two men’s talks ultimately stalling, and folding it into the clearer success story of the next year’s treaty. As the film’s single most lumpen line of dialogue reminds us at the close: “A journey of a thousand miles doesn’t begin with the most incredible arms deal in history — it begins with a single step.” Gunn’s film, on the other hand, is content to skip a few steps where necessary.

schema.headline: ‘The Brink of War’ Review: Reagan and Gorbachev Engage in Unengaging Verbal Battle

title: ‘Assassin’s Creed’ Creator’s New Action-Adventure Game ‘1666: Amsterdam’ Sets Early Access Release (Gaming News Roundup)
description:
Panache Digital Games announced “1666: Amsterdam” will release in Early Access on Aug. 25.

	From “Assassin’s Creed” series creator Patrice Désilets
body:
Panache Digital Games announced “1666: Amsterdam” will release in Early Access on Aug. 25.

	From “Assassin’s Creed” series creator Patrice Désilets, the dark, third-person narrative action-adventure game unravels a mystery across Amsterdam. Players take on the role of Noa, the Collector, who wields witchcraft to uncover “Originals,” demonic entities hiding behind human faces.

	The Early Access version of “1666: Amsterdam” will be available for PC via Steam and Epic Games Store for $29.99 on Aug. 25. The EA edition “will include the first piece of the campaign, expected to take approximately 15 hours to playthrough.” 
	

	Per the description for the game, “A cycle is ending. Another one is beginning. Take part in Noa’s Commencement as she inherits the mantle of the Collector. Unravel a mystery that spans centuries. Choose the companion that will walk beside you. Follow the traces left behind in a city shaped by secrets, power, and memory. This is where everything begins.”


	Watch a new gameplay feature for “1666: Amsterdam” below. The video gives an in-depth look at the game’s mechanics, combat and the day and night cycle. It also showcases the unique playing styles of lead characters Noa and Aaron as they hunt Originals across Amsterdam.



	See more gaming news from this week in the roundup below.
	
		AWARDS	

	The 2027 BAFTA Games Awards are now open for entries, albeit with a few key changes.

	BAFTA will now open the Evolving Game category to a member-wide vote across all rounds, while the organization has reaffirmed its commitment to “outstanding human achievement” in the face of concerns around AI. Entry fees have also been revised, with a new 25% discount for eligible independent and small developers.
	

	“With this year’s updates to eligibility and voting, the Awards continue to celebrate outstanding human creativity, craft and innovation, while evolving to reflect the way the sector is changing,” BAFTA’s director of awards Kelly Smith said in a statement. “I’m looking forward to seeing the exceptional work that will be recognized in 2027.”

	Entries will close on Friday, Sept. 18 for games released between November 15, 2025 and July 31, 2026, while entries will close on Friday, November 6 for games released between Aug. 1 and November 19, 2026.
	
		MONETIZATION	

	Mobile game developer and publisher Scopely announced a content creator initiative for “Monopoly Go!”

	The Go! Friends Creator Fund allows content creators to develop original ideas that adapt the themes of “Monopoly Go!’”s gameplay into their storytelling formats. 

	“At its core, Monopoly Go! is designed to give friends new reasons to connect, compete and have fun together. That same idea is the creative starting point for the GO! Friends Creator Fund,” said Jamie Berger, senior vice president of marketing for Monopoly Go! at Scopely. “We believe in providing creators with freedom to explore the themes of friendship in their own voice and format, while staying true to what works for their audience. Our goal is to move beyond one-off, transactional partnerships and build original entertainment alongside creators, and we’re excited to welcome more of them into the Monopoly Go! universe.”

	The fund supports creators artistic direction for their audiences, rather than relying on predetermined campaigns.
	
		EXEC SHUFFLE	

	Sandbox Group has appointed senior brand and entertainment marketing executive Amanda Klecker as chief marketing officer. 

	Klecker will oversee marketing and brand strategy across the life skill platform’s digital portfolio. She previously served as the head of marketing and franchise at pocket.watch, as well as working in marketing leadership at ViacomCBS/Paramount and Martha Stewart. Throughout her career, she’s received accolades such as Chief Marketer Top Women in Marketing: Disruptors, Cynopsis Top Women in Marketing: Marketing Trailblazers and 40 Under 40: NYC TV Week. 

	The platform’s global digital portfolio has 50 million monthly users, 1 billion app downloads and 500 monthly page views. Its flagship brands include PlayKids Learning, Coolmath Games and Focus.

schema.headline: ‘Assassin’s Creed’ Creator’s New Action-Adventure Game ‘1666: Amsterdam’ Sets Early Access Release (Gaming News Roundup)

title: Nicholas Hoult to Play Gilderoy Lockhart in ‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Season 2
description:
Nicholas Hoult will play Gilderoy Lockhart in the second season of HBO‘s “Harry Potter” TV series, Variety has learned from sources.

	The highly-an
body:
Nicholas Hoult will play Gilderoy Lockhart in the second season of HBO‘s “Harry Potter” TV series, Variety has learned from sources.

	The highly-anticipated series is due to debut on Dec. 25 on HBO and HBO Max, with the first season adapting the first book in the novel series, “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone.” The show has already been renewed for a second season, which will be based on “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.” 
	

	Lockhart is a central character in “Chamber of Secrets.” As the book begins, he is a famous wizard known for many heroic acts that he has documented in a number of books, though he is also incredibly arrogant and vain. He becomes the new Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher at Hogwarts, but it quickly becomes evident he is not qualified for the job.


	Lockhart was previously played by Kenneth Branagh in the “Chamber of Secrets” movie in 2002. 

	This will be Hoult’s latest appearance in a major franchise. He previously played Dr. Hank McCoy/Beast in multiple X-Men films, and currently plays Lex Luthor in James Gunn’s DC Studios films. He originated the latter role in “Superman” in 2025 and will reprise it in the sequel “Man of Tomorrow” in 2027.

	Hoult is also known for his roles in films like “Mad Max: Fury Road,” “Nosferatu,” “Juror #2,” “The Menu,” and “Renfield.” In television, he previously starred in the critically-acclaimed Hulu series “The Great,” for which he earned both an Emmy nomination and two Golden Globe nominations. He also played Luthor in the second season of “Peacemaker,” and had an early breakout role in the UK teen drama “Skins.” 
	

	He is repped by UTA, 42, and Sloane Offer. 

	Filming on the second season of “Harry Potter” is due to begin this fall. Dominic McLaughlin is set to play the title role in the show, with Arabella Stanton and Alastair Stout playing Hermione Granger and Ron Weasley. Additional cast members include John Lithgow as Hogwarts headmaster Dumbledore while Janet McTeer is Professor McGonagall, Paapa Essiedu plays Snape and Nick Frost has been cast as Rubeus Hagrid. 

	Jon Brown, a writer on the first season of the adaptation, has been promoted to serve as co-showrunner on Season 2. He joins current showrunner and series developer Francesca Gardiner. Gardiner serves as executive producer alongside director Mark Mylod. “Harry Potter” author J.K. Rowling also executive produces along with Neil Blair and Ruth Kenley-Letts of Brontë Film and TV and David Heyman of Heyday Films. Warner Bros. Television is the studio.

schema.headline: Nicholas Hoult to Play Gilderoy Lockhart in ‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Season 2

title: Rod Stewart Cancels Upcoming Tour Dates Following Coronary Stent Procedure
description: Rod Stewart has announced that he will be canceling the next four weeks of performances as part of his “One Last Time” farewell tour and “The Encore
body:
Rod Stewart has announced that he will be canceling the next four weeks of performances as part of his “One Last Time” farewell tour and “The Encore Shows” Las Vegas residency after undergoing a routine coronary stent procedure.

	The news comes just days after the singer postponed a show scheduled for Cincinnati’s Riverbend Music Center at the last minute, citing a “minor medical procedure.” Now, a rep for Stewart said that he underwent the procedure and that doctors are “pleased with his recovery.” The rep notes that he has returned to normal daily activities, but that he will need to recover before continuing to perform live.
	

	“I’m already feeling better and very much on the mend,” said Stewart, 81, in a statement. “I want to thank the doctors, nurses and everyone who has taken such wonderful care of me. I’m deeply disappointed to miss these shows and sorry to let my fans down, but I look forward to getting back on stage and having a good time with you all again soon.”


	In early June, Stewart canceled two performances in Las Vegas before showtime following his doctor’s advice. Later that month, he canceled another show in San Diego just before he was set to take the stage, and at a subsequent concert in Utah, he paused mid-show to use an oxygen tank backstage.

	Stewart has been on his “One Last Time” tour with Richard Marx since 2024. He had plans to perform tonight at Cleveland’s Rocket Arena, which announced the show cancellation yesterday, and this Saturday at Kansas City’s Morton Amphitheater. He was also scheduled to return to Vegas on August 18 for a string of shows at the Colosseum at Caesars Palace through the end of the month before heading back on the road for dates in Minnesota, Illinois and Mexico.
	

	Information regarding the affected performances will be shared by the venues and promoters involved with Stewart’s shows.

schema.headline: Rod Stewart Cancels Upcoming Tour Dates Following Coronary Stent Procedure

title: Zoe Saldaña Says It’s ‘Frustrating’ When Political Questions Only Get Asked to Actors of Color and Women: ‘That’s Incredibly Limiting’
description: Zoe Saldaña is growing frustrated with political questions, mainly because she doesn’t find them being asked in equal measure across the industry. T
body:
Zoe Saldaña is growing frustrated with political questions, mainly because she doesn’t find them being asked in equal measure across the industry. The Oscar winner said during a conversation at the Locarno Film Festival that she often participates in Q&As because she is eager to talk about the craft of acting. However, Saldaña keeps finding herself fielding political questions instead.

	“One thing that’s incredibly limiting, and frustrating, is when I’m the only person of color or the only woman on stage, and that happens quite a lot for women and for people of color. And I wait for my turn to be asked a question about my craft, and I’m asked the political question,” Saldaña said, giving the following example: “What do you think we need to do to make films more inclusive?”
	

	“I’m sorry, you don’t ask the only person that comes from the marginalized community,” Saldaña noted. “You ask the other 80 of them that are part of the gatekeepers, and you ask them if they know the answer because I think that we’re making people of color work double to be in a room.”

	Saldaña did not give any specific examples of press tours where she’s been inundated with political questions when compared to her co-stars and crew, although she was notably asked about “Emilia Perez” offending Mexicans just minutes after she won the best supporting actress Oscar in 2025.

	A journalist in the Oscars press room told Saldaña that the movie had been “really hurtful for us Mexicans,” to which the actor responded: “First of all, I’m very, very sorry that many Mexicans felt offended. That was never our intention. We spoke from a place of love. I don’t share your opinion. For me, the heart of this movie was not Mexico. We were making a film about friendship. We were making a film about four women.”
	

	“These women could have been Russian, could have been Dominican, could have been Black from Detroit, could have been from Israel, could have been from Gaza. And these women are still very universal women that are struggling every day, but trying to survive systemic oppression and trying to find the most authentic voices,” she added at the time. “So I will stand by that, but I’m also always open to sit down with all of my Mexican brothers and sisters, with love and respect, [to have] a great conversation on how ‘Emilia Pérez’ could have been done better. I welcome it.”

	Saldaña currently stars in the third season of “Lioness,” streaming on Paramount+. She attended the Locarno Film Festival this year and received a Special Honorary Pardo from festival director Giona Nazzaro. Click here for more highlights from her discussion.

schema.headline: Zoe Saldaña Says It’s ‘Frustrating’ When Political Questions Only Get Asked to Actors of Color and Women: ‘That’s Incredibly Limiting’

title: The Writers Lab Adds Los Angeles-Based Intensive, Announces Writers for Fall 2026 Cohorts
description:
The Writers Lab announced writers selected for two Lab Intensives this Fall, in New York City and the inaugural Los Angeles cohort.

	Supported by M
body:
The Writers Lab announced writers selected for two Lab Intensives this Fall, in New York City and the inaugural Los Angeles cohort.

	Supported by Meryl Streep and Nicole Kidman, The Writers Lab is the only script incubation program dedicated to elevating the work of women and nonbinary screenwriters over the age of 40.

	The Los Angeles cohort will gather at Women In Film and American Film Institute in October, with the New York cohort at Writers Guild of America East and Lincoln Center in November. Over three days, each program will focus on tools and strategies to build sustainable careers. Each intensive will be followed by a 5-day writing residency, enabling even more writers to develop and build industry connections.
	

	The Los Angeles participants are:


	Maja Costa“Terra Roxa” (Feature Historical Thriller)

	Jennifer Derwingson-Peacock “Fear Us Women” (One-Hour War Drama)

	Aurora Ferlin“13 Prisons” (One-Hour Drama/Mystery)

	Jessica Maison“Pirate Sea” (One-Hour Sci-Fi Adventure)

	Liz McClintock“Santa Susana” (Half-Hour Political Dramedy)

	Sarah Page“Vanilla” (One-Hour Comedy Thriller)

	Elise Shin“Perpetual Dreaming” (One-Hour Sci-Fi Thriller)

	Don Angelica Silva“Bright Belt” (Feature Historical Drama)

	The New York participants are:

	Wendy Bednarz“Glacial Summer” (Feature Coming-of-Age Drama)

	Michelle Bonnard“Superhuman” (Feature Drama)

	Rebecca Brown“A Forgotten Sky” (One-Hour Historical)

	Kate Chrisman“Foreign Correspondent” (One-Hour Political Thriller)
	

	Georgia Fu“Approximate Joy” (Feature Crime Dramedy)

	Courtney Graham“Nobody’s Horses” (One-Hour Historical Drama)

	Meghan Lennox“Gay for Amy” (Feature Coming-of-Age Comedy)

	Charise Studesville“The Waves” (Feature Dramedy)

	2026 mentors include Susan Cartsonis (“What Women Want,” “The Duff”), Anya Epstein (“The Affair,” “In Treatment”), Amy Fox (“The Connors,” “Equity”), Pamela Gray (“Megan Leavey,” “A Walk on the Moon”), Jenny Halper (“Unicorns,” “American Honey”), Rita Hsiao (“Mulan,” “The Monkey King”), Meg Lefauve (“Inside Out,” “My Father’s Dragon”), Amenya Makuku (FilmNation, “Madeline’s Madeline”), Mary Jane Skalski (“Hello I Must Be Going,” “The Visitor”), Amber Sealey (“No Man of God,” “Out of My Mind”), Robin Swicord (“The Curious Case of Benjamin Button,” “Memoirs of a Geisha”), Pat Verducci (Disney/Pixar, “True Crime”) and Jamie Zelermyer (Focus Features, “Boys Don’t Cry”).

	This year’s industry script jurors include Kyra Sedgwick (“Carolina Caroline,” “The Closer”), Clea Lewis (“Best Medicine”) and representatives from Blossom Films, Tribeca Studios and The Writers Guild of America East.

	New partners this year include Alliance of Women Directors, Women in Film LA, American Film Institute and Film at Lincoln Center. Other partners include The Writers Guild of America East, New York Women in Film & Television, Roadmap Writers, The Black List and Film Fatales.

	The third Lab Intensive will be offered in Canada in January 2027. TWL is in the process of developing an Intensive in Australia for 2027.

schema.headline: The Writers Lab Adds Los Angeles-Based Intensive, Announces Writers for Fall 2026 Cohorts

title: How Vera Drew, Louise Weard and More Trans and Nonbinary Filmmakers Are Taking Control of Their Stories Outside the Studio System: ‘We’re Creating a New Industry’
description: When Vera Drew made her ambitious debut film “The People’s Joker,” she didn’t know if anyone else in the world would understand her deeply personal
body:
When Vera Drew made her ambitious debut film “The People’s Joker,” she didn’t know if anyone else in the world would understand her deeply personal superhero movie parody about transitioning.

	The first time she met a trans person who connected with the film after a public screening was a “mindblowing” experience.

	“There had been other trans directors, but something that was that fiercely independent and coming at it from this personal perspective of a trans coming out story – I didn’t really know if there was any sort of audience for that,” Drew tells Variety. “I kind of just thought I was making a movie for myself.”
	

	Like many trans and nonbinary filmmakers making original, often genre-leaning films that resonate with queer audiences, Drew began connecting with other like-minded creatives after screening “The People’s Joker” at festivals like the Toronto International Film Festival and Fantastic Fest. Outside of online spaces, LGBTQ+ festivals like Outfest and Frameline have provided the necessary third spaces for this filmmaking community to grow.


	From Jane Schoenbrun (“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma”), Louise Weard (“Castration Movie”), Alice Maio Mackay (“The Serpent’s Skin”), Avalon Fast (“Camp”) to Drew (“The People’s Joker”), the past five years have brought this emerging group of trans and nonbinary artists into the spotlight. They often appear in each other’s projects and, for the most part, are all navigating the challenges of making art entirely outside the traditional studio system.
	

	Schoenbrun, for instance, appears in the third “Castration Movie” and Jack Haven’s short films. Weard has a role in “Camp Miasma,” while Fast acts in both “Castration Movie” and “The Serpent’s Skin.”

	“You get these communities together where we cannot only cheer each other on, but inform each other’s work and inspire one another,” Drew says. “Not every filmmaker has that in this dystopian version of Hollywood that the last generation of filmmakers manifested for all of us.”

	These artists are working in an industry that continually struggles to create space for trans and nonbinary filmmakers, from financing to theatrical distribution.

	A recent GLAAD report titled “Where We Are in Film” found that there were zero trans characters featured in 2025 releases from the top 10 U.S. distributors; this lack of representation, in large part, comes from a lack of trans directors making big budget movies. That representation shrinks even more when looking at trans directors of color.

	“Executives have to step up, not only to increase representation, but to maintain relevance with audiences. Gen Z is largely saving the box office and movie theaters, and they are the queerest generation of all time,” says Raina Deerwater, GLAAD’s associate director of entertainment research.

	“There’s a homogeneity to the type of trans filmmaker we’re seeing succeed right now that’s not 100% reflective of the diversity of the trans community,” Weard adds.

	One trans filmmaker who has made strides with bigger-budget features is Schoenbrun. Their horror comedy “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” which stars Gillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder, began its theatrical run this past weekend following a high-profile world premiere at Cannes.



	

					Sepi Mashiahof, Jane Schoenbrun and Gillian Anderson on set for “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.”
									David Astorga/Mubi
	



	As the Mubi release prepares to go wide later this month, Schoenbrun says they are conscious of their position within the industry as the rare trans filmmaker making movies at the $10 million mark.

	“I carry a lot of guilt about taking the money that I am obviously desperately clutching for from Hollywood. I’m really so proud of the movies I make, the way that I make them and the people I make them with. But being the only trans filmmaker making movies at this budget level — that’s not my fault, but it would be a lot better, in general, if I wasn’t the only one,” Schoenbrun says, explaining that they’ve felt “jealous” when watching directors like Mackay make movies with “a bunch of other trans people.”
	

	“And then even saying that out loud to you in Variety feels like, what an asshole thing to do! I could do that if I wanted to do that, but I’m choosing not to. I’m choosing to participate in this noxious system without any other people like me,” they add. “I have carved out a path that’s different from a lot of my trans peers, and that should just be part of the conversation.”

	The film that connects this circle of trans and nonbinary filmmakers most closely is Weard’s “Castration Movie” anthology, the third of which explores what happens in a relationship after Izzy’s (Fast) partner comes out as trans — an experience that has rarely been depicted in film.

	Throughout all three “Castration” chapters, Weard says she has been drawn to “ugly perspectives” in the world.

	“With this one, the idea of the TERF and the type of person who would claim feminism at the expense of trans people’s rights is a perspective very distant from mine,” Weard says. “In researching the role, it came down to this idea of equating male violence with this fear of trans people, where these women might see a trans woman as the scary men in their life who have preyed on them in the past.”

	Weard’s DIY-style anthology has become a crucial epicenter of contemporary trans artists, featuring everyone from Schoenbrun to Drew to Mackay in various roles. Lilly Wachowski even executive produced the third chapter.

	Weard also embraces the perspective of a trans character that’s “hard to understand” at times. “She’s this totem for the embarrassing start of transition that I think a lot of trans people go through.”

	As one of the most prolific trans filmmakers making movies right now, Schoenbrun takes the initiative to have emerging directors and writers shadow on set. Eva Victor, for instance, shadowed on “I Saw the TV Glow” before going on to write and direct their award-winning indie breakout “Sorry, Baby,” while “The Serpent’s Skin” and “Our Effed Up World” director Mackay shadowed on “Camp Miasma.”

	Mackay says, “We’re not competing with each other; we’re all trying to do our own thing but have this community to lean back and be supported on.”

	After making “We’re All Going to the World’s Fair,” which put Schoenbrun on the map in 2021 after Sundance, they have intentionally placed “more boundaries” around them.
	

	“Even while I have a circle of really close friends and artists who I admire and love and want to be collaborating with and supporting in this way, there’s something that’s always going to be a little transactional about it,” Schoenbrun says.

	Thanks to the Fatales Forward program, emerging filmmaker Sepi Mashiahof was matched with Schoenbrun as a mentor. Since then, Mashiahof worked as Schoenbrun’s assistant on “I Saw the TV Glow” and was promoted to script coordinator on “Camp Miasma.”

	“What I learned from Jane is how much they love and are so open and receptive to the ideas of the people around them,” Mashiahof says.

	Haven, who starred in both “I Saw the TV Glow” and “Camp Miasma” and has directed multiple short films, explains that they’ve seen Schoenbrun take “great pains” to raise money.

	“This comes from explaining themselves, through working really diligently to connect with financiers about this universal pain that they work into their films, and I think there’s something in it that cannot be bought or sold,” Haven says. “Of course, we are connected to an industry that is about making money, that is about self-sustaining as artists, but ultimately it becomes more and more about what cannot be bought or sold and what is eternal to us as artists.”

	Schoenbrun’s experience as an openly trans filmmaker is deeply reflected in their work, particularly with the journey that “Camp Miasma” protagonist Kris (Hannah Einbinder) takes in fighting to get her vision understood by studio executives.

	Schoenbrun explains: “Anytime I’m on a Zoom with Hollywood, with people who I’m maybe going to work with on something, or doing a general, my transness is going to be in the room. Even if they have the best intentions, it’s a particular minority experience in that there are no other trans people on the other side of the call. And if there is, it’s queer assistant, right? And they’re not actually being given any power, they’re there in a tokenized way.”

	Drew says she’d “love” to make a studio movie, for one. But getting a second feature off the ground has proven difficult.

	“My first movie was a huge critical success, got a ton of buzz out of its festival run, had a Streisand effect because of its legal baggage, it won multiple awards,” Drew says. “In another era, that probably could have meant that Disney or Paramount or fucking Star Wars, one of these people would be coming to me and saying, ‘We have this thing we want you to shepherd.’”
	

	She continues: “I don’t know if I’m just too aggressive and trans and hairy-arm pitted for that to happen, but I do know that didn’t happen to me — I assume kind of partially because of media consolidation, also because of the subject matter of my first movie. And the fact that I made a movie that was very explicitly about my experience as a trans woman and as an artist, which is another thing that makes it quasi-inaccessible to a major studio.”

	Drew’s next feature, the horror comedy “Trandemic,” recently earned a $25,000 cash grant from the Duplass Brothers’ inaugural Found Footage Feature Fund award, and has reportedly already attracted interest from distributors. Other programs like the Trans Film Mentorship and the Sundance Institute’s Trans Possibilities Intensive also provide funding for trans filmmakers.

	In addition to performing in films like “Castration Movie” and “Camp Miasma,” Fast is a filmmaker in their own right, making their debut with “Honeycomb” back in 2022 for just $5,000 with a group of friends.

	Their most recent film, “Camp,” follows a troubled young woman who works as a camp counselor to escape the memory of tragic events in her life. Things, of course, take a supernatural, witchy turn.



	

					A still from Avalon Fast’s “Camp.”
									Courtesy of MPI Media
	



	Despite getting a higher budget for “Camp,” which was distributed by Dark Sky Films and played at festivals like Frameline, Fast doesn’t have any ambitions to work with more money on future projects.

	“I really want to have a good life and I don’t want my life to become industrialized. We all know how bad it is, so why are we fighting to be a part of it?” Fast says. “For me, I’m able to sustain myself through service work, I’m comfortable doing that, I don’t mind it. If I can continue making films for micro budgets with my friends, these are the things that I find inspiring and that I get real joy out of.”

	Even with “Camp,” Fast admits they had a “really hard time” maintaining their voice.

	“I’m so opposed to sacrificing any of my vision for something to be better understood or for our distributors to be happy or for the producers to feel involved in the process or whatever,” Fast says. “I got ‘Camp’ through to the other side without the vision being too mangled, but fuck, it was such a fight. And I don’t want to fight my whole life when I don’t have to.”
	

	Mackay, who at the age of 22 has already directed seven features, recently screened “Our Effed Up World” at Fantastia, which was produced by Schoenbrun. To date, she has heavily relied on crowdfunding to bring her projects to life.

	“I feel very grateful to have been able to make the films I have made, but it’s been at such a micro scale. I don’t necessarily want to do the next Marvel movie and have a trillion dollars, but I want to make something in the few million-dollar range,” Mackay says. “That’s the dream to keep growing and moving out of the micro-budget space.”

	Many of Mackay’s films are streaming on Shudder, which has helped her body of work connect with horror fans around the world.

	“I mean, they literally picked up my first film that I made with no money when I was 16, and that was not something that I ever dreamed of,” Mackay says.

	As if making movies wasn’t already hard enough, trans storytellers working in independent spaces are now grappling with the realities of a shifting industry in which studios are consolidating, leading many in Hollywood to sign open letters speaking out against the looming Paramount-Warner Bros. merger. The merger has also ignited fears about a rightward shift.

	But the reality is that many trans and nonbinary filmmakers have already had to carve out a space for themselves separate from the studio system.

	“This literal monopoly that’s existed, to me, adds value to independent filmmakers. I think independent film is stronger than ever,” Drew says. “The capitalist hellscape that we’re in makes me feel more empowered as an independent filmmaker because my perspective has value.”

	Alex Schmider, GLAAD’s senior director of entertainment and a producer behind “Disclosure” and “Changing the Game,” says he is “inspired” by contemporary trans artists: “They are undeterred by lack of funding, institutional support, and traditional distribution. In fact, they’re more creative and collaborative in their approach and strategies than ever.”

	Drew says: “The benefit of mostly existing in these indie spaces is that we get to tell our own story and get to control the narrative a little bit. I make the movies that only I could make. Louise makes the movies that only she could, and Alice is the same way.”
	

	There was a wave not too long ago when Hollywood tried to tell stories about trans people, usually helmed by cisgender directors. Several won Oscars, including “The Danish Girl” starring Eddie Redmayne and “Boys Don’t Cry” starring Hilary Swank. But in today’s media landscape, no directors working with major studios are interested.

	“When I’ve pitched ideas in mainstream spaces and there is a trans lead, the feedback I’ve gotten sometimes is, ‘This is too niche.’ Which is frustrating, I guess, but it’s only frustrating because it appeared differently when the trans tipping point was happening with ‘Transparent’ on TV.”

	A recent example of a cisgender director prominently centering their film around a trans character was Jacques Audiard’s musical “Emilia Pérez.” Despite earning 13 Oscar nominations, that film faced significant pushback from the LGBTQ+ community.

	Haven says, “It’s a film from the voyeuristic perspective, and so it makes transness into something that is fascinating, titillating, perverse. But it doesn’t hit at the core of what I understand transness to be, which is in direct opposition to the message that things cannot change. Because transness is imagination, and imagination is liberation.”

	Mashiahof adds that when cisgender directors tell trans stories, they happen to align with the “strange imagination” that a man is pretending to be a woman.

	“Whereas you have a film like ‘I Saw the TV Glow’ where transness is just this feeling that is the world, versus it being located on a person doing a thing that looks weird to society,” Mashiahof says. “When trans filmmakers are given the opportunity to tell a story, it actually warps that and shifts the onus of that weirdness onto society versus the person.”

	Born out of filmmaker and programmer Elizabeth Purchell’s “moment of crisis,” Muscle Distribution was founded in 2025 as the only trans-owned distribution label. In the past year, Muscle has become the go-to stop for micro-budget films from trans filmmakers like “Castration Movie,” as well as two of Fast’s films, “Honeycomb” and the upcoming release “Drinking and Driving.”

	“The ultimate gimmick is seeing a trans movie in a theater because they’re not really being made, programmers aren’t showing them and no one wants to get behind them in a meaningful way,” Purchell says. “[But] now we’re in this moment where there is this opening for people to find stuff online, for DIY groups to put together screenings, for theaters and festivals to start taking notice. Something really is happening.”
	

	Some filmmakers in this space have also taken the approach of making their films widely available  online with a “pay what you wish” model, which Weard has done with all three “Castration” films. 

	“It was definitely a project that was always designed for online first. Anything else has been a fun bonus,” she says.



	

					A behind-the-scenes still from “Castration Movie Anthology III: Year of the Hyaena.”
									Courtesy Photo
	



	Weard, who started making movies over a decade ago, has noticed “so much more hope” in the trans filmmakers she meets now.

	“I was just at the Cannes Film Festival and I saw so many trans people walking around at the market and at these pavilions,” she says. “I was so blown away. That was not an experience I was seeing at all at film festivals a few years ago.”

	Looking around at the community they’ve found and the work their friends are putting out against the odds, Haven says that “we’re creating a new industry.”

	“I think there’s a lot of power in it because it can’t be co-opted and it can’t be bought,” they conclude. “We went through a really confusing era where big industry was trying to take transness and sell it to us, but it actually just doesn’t sell because transness threatens a lot of the structures that we know. We are in a place, now, where we’re able to reinvent it on our own.”

schema.headline: How Vera Drew, Louise Weard and More Trans and Nonbinary Filmmakers Are Taking Control of Their Stories Outside the Studio System: ‘We’re Creating a New Industry’

title: Fans Remember Jackie the Eagle, Who Became a Social Media Star Worldwide: ‘Regal, Fierce, Deeply Devoted’
description: Los Angeles media has been all over the death of a local celebrity for the past two days. But this time, the dearly departed wasn’t a movie star fro
body:
Los Angeles media has been all over the death of a local celebrity for the past two days. But this time, the dearly departed wasn’t a movie star from the golden age of Hollywood. Instead, Southern Californians and the rest of the world are mourning the death of Jackie, the bald eagle. Jackie, who lived with her partner Shadow in a nest high above the mountain community of Big Bear, died Monday after several weeks in intensive care.

	For the past decade, a Big Bear webcam that broadcast the lives of Jackie and her partner Shadow has drawn viewers from around the world, garnering 822,000 subscribers on YouTube and over a million Facebook followers. Eagle fans watched Jackie’s arrival in the nest, the death of an earlier set of eaglets, and Shadow aggressively kicking out Jackie’s earlier partner. (They’re currently watching closely to see if Shadow may have already moved in a new partner, observing practically no mourning period.)
	

	Los Angeles-area news outlets including KNBC, KTLA and others featured news reports Monday night and into Tuesday about the outpouring of support for Jackie. The response from animal lovers both in California and worldwide has nearly approached the reaction to the death of mountain lion P-22, who was euthanized in 2022 and has since been memorialized with an annual festival and a line of merch benefiting the parks department.  


	The eagle’s fans included actress Holly Robinson Peete, who wrote, “She was regal, fierce, and deeply devoted. Jackie made millions of us care about one nest in a tree like it was our own backyard.”
	

	California senator Adam Schiff also paid tribute, writing, “Devastated to learn of the passing of California’s pride, Jackie, earlier today. Any visitor to my Washington office in the past year knows our office proudly showed the livestream of Jackie’s nest showing alongside C-SPAN and national news.”

	Jackie, who was estimated to be about 14 years old, recently hatched two eaglets, Sandy and Luna, who have already flown the nest after their April birth. Jackie was found grounded after a fight with younger eagles in July, and may have already been ill, according to veterinarians. She had also been suffering from anemia.

	The Ojai Raptor Center released a statement, saying “Throughout her time at Ojai Raptor Center, every decision was guided by the available medical evidence, her welfare, and our responsibility to do what was in her best interest. Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her.”

	Could a feature deal — or at least a documentary — about the life and loves of Jackie be far away?

schema.headline: Fans Remember Jackie the Eagle, Who Became a Social Media Star Worldwide: ‘Regal, Fierce, Deeply Devoted’

title: Cinema Civil War: Why the Paramount-Warner Bros. Sale Is Dividing Movie Theater Owners
description: Movie theater owners have become embroiled in the kind of drama they usually sell on the big screen, thanks to the ongoing saga of Paramount’s propo
body:
Movie theater owners have become embroiled in the kind of drama they usually sell on the big screen, thanks to the ongoing saga of Paramount’s proposed takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.

	Cinema United, the exhibition industry’s main lobbying group, for months has been publicly opposed to any potential sale of Warner Bros. The trade organization’s president, Michael O’Leary, is concerned a merger will lead to fewer films and potential theater closures. He now has another problem: The group’s two most powerful members, AMC Theatres and Regal Cinemas, are contradicting that message.
	

	In a major blow to the org’s solidarity, the CEOs of the two largest theater chains, AMC’s Adam Aron and Regal’s Eduardo Acuna, are throwing their support behind the $111 billion deal. Insiders note that O’Leary, who became president and CEO of Cinema United in 2023, was appointed in part because he was viewed as less fiery than his predecessor, John Fithian, an outspoken advocate for theater owners. With O’Leary now out of step with his two biggest members, Cinema United’s smaller exhibitors worry about how the internal fracture might jeopardize their future bargaining power, should the pact knock out another major supplier.


	“This infighting is not good for anybody,” says one regional exhibitor. “Leadership can’t control the big guys, and it makes us all look like clowns. How do studios take you seriously if they don’t know who is running the ship?”

	Cinema United’s leadership isn’t blinking. O’Leary tells Variety the group’s “responsibility and commitment is to the entire exhibition community.” He adds, “As we have since the outset, we will continue to pursue opportunities for meaningful and enforceable guardrails to protect our industry for the future.”
	

	AMC and Regal declined to comment.

	Aron has been backing the merger since CinemaCon in April, arguing the combined company would strengthen the theatrical business. After a collection of state attorneys general filed an antitrust lawsuit last month to block the deal, Aron doubled down in a Variety op-ed, asserting the “complaint simply gets the economics of our business backwards.” Making matters more uncomfortable: Aron’s piece was published on the same day that O’Leary issued his own letter to endorse the litigation to delay the merger, writing “the promises of support for theatrical being made in the media are high-level and unenforceable and as such do nothing to alleviate the harms.”

	Then Acuna warned last week that delaying the merger might create “more uncertainty and distraction that could be damaging to our industry as we build on our current success.” Hollywood is enjoying its biggest summer season since COVID, and yearly domestic revenues are poised to hit $10 billion for the first time since 2019.

	Meanwhile, Sean Gamble, CEO of No. 3 U.S. chain Cinemark, hasn’t officially endorsed the merger.

	Cinema United’s leaders were blindsided by Aron’s support for the merger at CinemaCon, sources say, but many members saw his contradictory comments as par for the course, since Aron has diverged with Cinema United on prior issues. Now, with Regal also backing the deal, the group may be on the brink of a civil war.

	Aron and Acuna are disposed to favor the pending marriage because Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison has pledged the joint studio will release at least 30 films a year. By contrast, Disney and Universal, the two biggest studios by market share, each release 16-20 movies annually.

	O’Leary and others in Hollywood are skeptical of Ellison’s promise, pointing to the combined company’s substantial $80 billion debt load and plans to cut $6 billion in duplicative efforts across the business. Meanwhile, cinema operators haven’t yet recovered from the 2019 Disney-Fox merger, which resulted in fewer new releases.

	There’s a sense among industry insiders that Aron and Acuna believe the Paramount-Warner Bros. union is inevitable and want to stay on Ellison’s good side. Shortly after Acuna’s statement, Bloomberg reported that Ellison offered AMC and Regal a three-year, contractually enforceable agreement that would guarantee exclusive 45-day theatrical windows.
	

	“Paramount already guaranteed a 45-day window,” the indie operator points out. “I don’t see how that swung the tide.”

	Cinema United can still argue the health of the exhibition business rests on more than just AMC and Regal. Those large circuits each operate hundreds of locations, and, sure, they might be able to survive more consolidation. However, more than 90% of Cinema United members have fewer than 75 screens. It’s the hundreds of independent theaters that will be vulnerable.

	“We will be faced with the same dilemma from Disney-Fox,” says another arthouse theater owner. “There were fewer films and therefore less competition to get on our screens, putting them in a controlling position. We’ve been told, ‘Take it or leave it.’”

schema.headline: Cinema Civil War: Why the Paramount-Warner Bros. Sale Is Dividing Movie Theater Owners

title: Ohio Mom, Two Partners Charged With Murder After 7-Year-Old Son Found Dead in Closet
description:

body:
Ohio Mom
                          Charged With Murder ...
                          7-Year-Old Son Found Dead in Closet
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 11, 2026
                            5:40 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            An Ohio mother and her two partners are facing murder charges after her 7-year-old son was found dead and duct-taped inside a closet ... with authorities alleging the boy endured horrific abuse before his death.
      
    
            Police found William Evans-Ellis Thursday inside a Cincinnati home shared by his mom, Kaitlin Evans, and her partners, Nessa Keaney, and Kirby Rankin.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hamilton County officials say William died from blunt force trauma to the head and had injuries across much of his body. Investigators allege he was beaten, burned, and subjected to water torture.
      

            The county coroner said she personally opened the closet where William was found and froze at the sight.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Evans, Keaney and Rankin were arrested and charged with murder and child endangerment. Evans' attorney says the defense believes another person charged in the case caused William's death.
      
    
            All three remain behind bars and a competency hearing will be held for Rankin in September.

title: ABC News Anchor Liz Cho Seeks Protective Order Against Ex-CBS Host Josh Elliott
description:

body:
ABC News Anchor Liz Cho
                          Files for Protective Order Against Ex-CBS Host Josh Elliott
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 11, 2026
                            5:43 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Liz Cho has filed for a protective order amid her contentious divorce from Josh Elliott ... but the request has nothing to do with her personal safety.
      
    
            The ABC7 New York news anchor asked the court to block Elliott's attorneys from deposing her on July 23, according to court documents obtained by Page Six.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Cho filed the request July 17, arguing the deposition had been scheduled without first checking whether she or her attorneys were available.
      

            "The deposition was noticed without any inquiry as to the availability of [Cho] and her counsel," the filing reportedly states.
      
    
            Cho claims she told the former CBS host's legal team her attorneys had previously scheduled conflicts and offered alternative dates ... but says Elliott's side never responded.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            It's unclear whether the deposition ultimately went forward or was rescheduled.
      
    
            Cho also objected to Elliott's request that she turn over communications with anyone other than him with whom she had a "romantic and/or sexual relationship" between July 2015 and June 2025.
      
    
            Despite her objection, the Daily Mail reports Cho turned over the requested documents during a virtual hearing on July 24.
      
    
            Elliott filed for divorce in June 2025, and the split has since turned into a messy legal battle.
